newsitem.title: FRANCE: France steps up fight against paedophilia.
newsitem.headline: France steps up fight against paedophilia.

text.p: France marked its first Children's Day on Wednesday by unveiling plans to toughen laws protecting minors against sex crimes and keep closer tabs on rapists.

The plan has acquired fresh urgency following Belgium's paedophilia scandal of kidnap and murder as well as several less publicised rapes and murders of children in France that have shocked public opinion.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe told a news conference called to present the plan that 5,500 children suffered sexual abuse in France last year, and another 60,000 were regarded as "in danger".

A society unable to protect "the weakest among the weak" should be seen as worthless, Juppe said. "We must let children understand that they have the power of screaming 'no, no and no' when they are being hurt," he added.
A main point in the plan is to try prevent sex convicts from becoming repeat criminals by keeping them under medical supervision for up to 10 years after they are released from jail.

They could be jailed again for breaking the rules of such supervision. Convicted paedophiles would be banned from jobs involving regular contacts with children, and from visiting places where minors hang out.
"Nothing is more inadmissible than the identical repeat of violence and sexual abuse against children by criminals who have already committed such offences," Juppe said.

Statistics say that up to 20 percent of rapists and 25 percent of paedophiles become repeat offenders after being released from prison. Experts say medical surveillance could cut the rate of recidivism by half.

The Belgian scandal began last August with the arrest of convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux and the subsequent rescue of two sexually abused girls, the discovery of the dead bodies of four more and the search for at least seven others.
The French plan, due to be put to the cabinet next month, also aims to fight sexual tourism and publication of pornography involving children.
It will ban sex shops from the vicinity of schools.
Possession of pornographic pictures of children would become a prosecutable offence as opposed to present laws which punish only distribution.
Using modern distribution techniques such as the worldwide Internet web or computer networks will be deemed an aggravating circumstance.
In order to keep an eye on cyber-networks, the minister for telecommunications will join a special ministerial group in charge of implementing the plan.
Teachers, magistrates and the police will be trained to spot whether children are being ill-treated. A public information campaign will be launched early next year.

A free phone number that battered or abused children may call for help will be widely publicised. To make sure that callers remain anonymous and do not suffer reprisals from parents, the number will be automatically deleted from telephone bills.
Children who have been mistreated will be accompanied by psychiatrists when they report to police. Their testimony will be video-taped so they do not have to confront their molesters.
